simple: Inside #Pactus #1: Pactus has a fixed supply: 42M PAC, all created at launch. Nothing new is ever minted. Half sits in a treasury that pays out block rewards over time. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #1: Pactus has a fixed supply of 42,000,000 PAC, all allocated in the genesis file. Half (21M) sits in the treasury, the all-zero address, and is paid out as block rewards. No minting: rewards come from this pre-allocated pot. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #2: A new Pactus block every 10 seconds, on a steady clock: block times always land on the same 10-second marks of each minute. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #2: Pactus block time is 10 seconds. A custom genesis is rejected if its interval doesn't divide 60, and block times must have a seconds field that's a multiple of the interval, so the 10 s slots line up the same way every minute. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #3: Block rewards shrink over time: 1 PAC per block at first, then 0.5, then 0.25, in steps tied to block count. They come from the 21M PAC treasury, which at these rates lasts until around block 44M. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #3: Pactus block reward (PIP-55), as coded: 1 PAC per block up to height 8M, 0.5 up to 24M, then 0.25. It depends on block height, not calendar time. Rewards come from the 21M PAC treasury, which at these rates runs out around block 44M. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #4: The first reward halving comes at block 8 million: about 2.5 years after launch in theory, later in practice, because blocks missed during slowdowns are not made up. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #4: First reward halving is at block 8,000,000: about 2.5 years after genesis if every 10 s slot got a block, the second (24M) about 7.6 years. Missed slots are not made up (a late block takes the current time), so real dates come later. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #5: Each block sends a small share of its reward to the foundation, rotating across 100 addresses. That share shrinks along with the reward. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #5: Every Pactus block pays a slice of its reward to a foundation address chosen as `height mod 100` from a list of 100 addresses. The base amount is 0.3 PAC and it halves with the block reward. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #6: Every block opens with one special transaction that pays the block reward from the treasury. Validators check that the amounts follow the rules before accepting the block. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #6: Every Pactus block starts with exactly one subsidy transaction: a zero-fee batch transfer from the treasury. Validators check it: the total must equal reward + fees, and the foundation payout and any delegation share must match the rules. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #7: Block times can't be faked: a block must come after the previous one and close to its expected slot. If the chain fell behind, the next block simply uses the current time. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #7: Timestamps aren't free-form: seconds must be a multiple of 10, and the time must follow the previous block and be at most one interval past the expected slot. If the chain is >10 s behind, the proposer uses current time, rounded down. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #8: Pactus mainnet launched on January 24, 2024. Since then: a block every 10 seconds, secured by a committee of 51 validators at a time. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #8: Pactus mainnet genesis time: 2024-01-24 20:24 UTC (testnet: 2024-03-16 00:00 UTC). Both networks use 10-second blocks and a committee of 51 validators. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #9: How does a node know which network it's on? It fingerprints the genesis file, the chain's birth certificate, and compares it with the known mainnet and testnet fingerprints. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #9: The genesis file has no chain ID field. A node hashes the genesis document and compares it to the built-in mainnet and testnet hashes; anything else is a localnet. That picks the address prefix and the p2p network name. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #10: Every block starts with a small header of exactly 138 bytes: time, who made it, and fingerprints of the previous block and of the whole chain state. Small and predictable. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #10: A block header is exactly 138 bytes: version (1), time (4), previous hash (32), state root (32), sortition seed (48), proposer address (21). Fixed layout, so a stored block's time is read at a known offset without decoding it. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #11: A block's ID covers its header, its parent's proof and a fingerprint of all its transactions. Change a single transaction and the block ID changes. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #11: A Pactus block hash covers the header, the previous certificate's hash, the transaction Merkle root and the tx count. Transactions enter the hash only through their root. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #12: Transactions are folded into one fingerprint (a Merkle root). Pactus also adds their count to the block ID, closing a known corner case of this kind of tree. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #12: Pactus's tx Merkle tree hashes an odd node with itself, so the root alone doesn't commit to the leaf count. The block hash adds the count separately to close that gap. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #13: A Pactus block holds at most 1,000 transactions, and nodes reject anything bigger while reading it, before even validating it. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #13: A Pactus block holds at most 1,000 transactions. The decoder rejects a length prefix above that before it allocates the transaction list, so the limit holds at parse time, not only during validation. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #14: Every block is approved by the committee, but the proof stays tiny: a list of who took part and one combined signature instead of dozens. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #14: A Pactus block certificate = height, round, committers (validator numbers), absentees and ONE aggregated BLS signature. No per-validator signatures on chain; the signers are "committers minus absentees". #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #15: Checking that a block was approved takes a single signature check, however many validators signed. That keeps nodes fast and light. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #15: Verifying a Pactus certificate takes one BLS check: sum the power of the signers, require 2f+1, aggregate their public keys, verify the single signature. No loop over individual signatures. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #16: Each block carries the proof that its parent was approved, so the chain links itself together, block after block, back to the first one. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #16: Each Pactus block embeds the aggregated certificate that finalised its parent, checked against the previous height's committee. Only the genesis block has none. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #17: Validators are referred to by a short number instead of a full address, so block proofs stay small even with a full committee. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #17: Certificates list validators by a compact number (int32, varint), not their 21-byte address. Numbers are sequential: genesis validators first, then each new validator when its first bond creates it. Small index, small certificate. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #18: Each kind of consensus vote signs a different message, so a vote cast for one step can never be reused for another. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #18: Every consensus vote signs block hash ‖ height ‖ round plus a type tag (PREPARE, PRE-VOTE, MAIN-VOTE, DECIDED; PRECOMMIT has none), and change-proposer votes add the CP round and value. No vote type can pass as another. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #19: Amounts and fees in a transaction have exactly one valid encoding, so every node reads, hashes and signs the very same bytes. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #19: Pactus votes are CBOR maps with fixed integer keys (1-7). Transaction amounts and fees are LEB128 varints, and the decoder rejects non-minimal varints, so each integer has exactly one byte encoding in a transaction. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #20: A transaction's ID depends only on what it says (amount, fee, memo…), not on its signature. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #20: A Pactus transaction ID is the hash of its signing bytes (version, lock time, fee, memo, payload) and excludes the signature. The ID depends only on what the transaction says. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #21: Pactus doesn't elect its validators by vote. After each block, every validator runs a private lottery, and the winners can claim a seat on the committee. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #21: Pactus doesn't vote its committee in. After every block each validator runs a private lottery with the chain seed. Winners broadcast a sortition tx to take a seat. Default committee size: 51. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #22: The committee lottery can't be rigged: each validator's ticket comes from its own key and the chain's randomness, and anyone can check it. One draw per validator per block. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #22: Pactus sortition proof = a BLS signature over (seed ‖ public key), hashed with BLAKE2b-256 and scaled into [0, total power). One seed, one deterministic output per key. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #23: More stake means better odds, but fairly: a validator with 10% of the stake wins about 10% of the lottery draws. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #23: In Pactus a validator wins sortition when its index is below its own power, with the range set to total network power. So a validator with 10% of the stake wins about 10% of the draws. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #24: Where does the randomness come from? Each block's proposer signs the previous random value to make the next one, and every node checks it. No one gets to choose it. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #24: Pactus randomness is a chain of BLS signatures: each block's sortition seed is the proposer's signature over the hash of the previous seed, and every node verifies it against the proposer's key before accepting the block. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #25: A lottery win must be claimed fast: the ticket expires after 17 blocks, about 3 minutes. Normal transactions stay valid for about a day. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #25: A Pactus sortition tx is only valid for a short window: 17 blocks (≈3 minutes). Other transactions get 8,640 blocks (≈1 day). #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #26: New validators wait about one hour after staking before they can enter the committee lottery. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #26: New Pactus validators wait 360 blocks (≈1 hour) after bonding before their sortition txs are accepted. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #27: The committee changes gradually: at each step, less than a third of its power can be replaced, and the members who leave are the longest-seated ones. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #27: Pactus bounds committee churn: when the committee is full, the power joining in one step must stay under one third of committee power, and the members who leave are the ones with the oldest sortition. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #28: While a validator sits on the committee, its stake is frozen: it can't add to it or unstake until it leaves. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #28: In Pactus your stake is frozen while you sit on the committee: bond and unbond txs for a member are rejected in block validation until the validator leaves. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #29: Validators take turns proposing blocks, round-robin. A newcomer joins at the back of the line. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #29: Proposer order is a round-robin walk over a linked list of committee members. New members are inserted just behind the current proposer, so they wait at the back of the queue until the rest of the committee has had a turn. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #30: A node that restarts doesn't need a saved copy of the committee: it rebuilds it from the latest blocks. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #30: Pactus restarts without a committee snapshot. The node rebuilds the committee from the last certificate and the sortition txs of the last block, then replays the rotation. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #31: A validator can stake up to 1,000 PAC. Each stake transaction must be at least 1 PAC, unless it tops the validator up to exactly 1,000. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #31: Pactus stake limits (defaults, same on mainnet): each bond must be at least 1 PAC and a validator's total stake can't exceed 1,000 PAC. A bond under 1 PAC is only accepted if it tops the validator up to exactly 1,000 PAC. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #32: In Pactus, voting weight = stake. Unstake and your validator's weight drops to zero right away. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #32: In Pactus, voting power = stake in nanoPAC (1 PAC = 10⁹), except genesis bootstrap validators, which have no stake and power 1. A validator that unbonds drops to zero power in the same block the unbond is executed. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #33: Unstaking takes 21 days: voting weight goes away at once, and the funds can be withdrawn three weeks later. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #33: Unbonding a Pactus validator removes its power immediately. The stake can be withdrawn after 181,440 blocks, i.e. 21 days. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #34: Unstaking and claiming a committee seat cost no fee at all. That's a protocol rule. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #34: Pactus unbond and sortition transactions carry a fee of exactly zero. It's a protocol rule enforced in basic validation, not only a mempool policy. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #35: Delegation (PIP-49): a stake owner can let an operator run the validator. The owner gets a capped share of the rewards, and only the owner can unstake, once the agreed period ends. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #35: PIP-49 delegation: a delegated bond is exactly the max stake (1,000 PAC) with a future expiry. Owner reward share is capped at 0.7 PAC/block (before halving). The owner, not the operator, signs unbond and withdraw; unbond only after expiry. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #36: How does Pactus upgrade? Validators signal by running the new version. Once more than 75% of committee stake supports it, blocks switch to the new version. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #36: Protocol upgrades (PIP-51) are signalled by stake: a proposer moves to the new block version only once >75% of committee power runs a node that supports it. No scheduled activation height (the PIP-55 halving is height-based). #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #37: Pactus upgrades so far: split rewards, delegation, reward halving and on-chain anchoring, each one a numbered protocol version. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #37: Pactus protocol versions so far: v2 split reward (PIP-43), v3 delegation (PIP-49), v4 halving (PIP-55), v5 native state anchoring (PIP-50). One enum value per upgrade. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #38: Pactus consensus counts stake, not heads: a block needs approval from validators holding a supermajority, about two thirds, of committee stake. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #38: Pactus counts BFT quorums in voting power (stake), not head count. With n = total power, f = (n-1)/3. The v2 consensus code checks f+1, 2f+1 and 3f+1 of it; block certificates need 2f+1. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #39: The next version of Pactus consensus (v2 code) removes one voting step, so a block gets approved with one round of votes fewer. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #39: Pactus's v2 consensus code (consensusv2) drops the prepare phase: a block goes straight from proposal to precommit. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #40: If a block proposer is slow, validators vote to replace it. They wait 5 seconds, then 10, then 15 in later rounds, or start sooner if enough of them already agree. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #40: Pactus's change-proposer timeout grows linearly: 5 s + 5 s per round (round 0: 5 s, round 1: 10 s, round 2: 15 s), counted from the start of the round. A validator can start earlier if it already sees f+1 change-proposer pre-votes. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #41: Replacing a slow proposer is a vote of its own, in up to three steps. Each vote must carry a proof of why it was cast, which the other validators check. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #41: The change-proposer phase has three vote types: pre-vote, main-vote, decided, each with a justification others check. Values are Yes (change proposer) or No (keep it); only main-votes can be Abstain. It repeats in CP rounds until decided. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #42: In the v2 code, if almost the whole committee (by stake) approves a block, it is committed right away, with no extra voting round. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #42: v2 fast path: once a validator holds the proposal and sees precommits for it from 3f+1 of total voting power, it commits with no change-proposer round. With only 2f+1 precommits, the change-proposer phase must decide "No" first. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #43: Validators that are often offline lose their turn: if a proposer's availability score is below two thirds, the committee moves straight to replacing it. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #43: In Pactus, if the scheduled proposer's availability score is below 0.666667 (PIP-19), validators skip the proposal and go straight to changing the proposer for that round. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #44: Each validator has an availability score: how often it showed up while on the committee, over roughly the last week. Computed from the chain, not self-reported. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #44: A validator's availability score = 1 − (certificates it was absent from ÷ certificates it was in the committee for), over the last 60,000 certificates (≈6.9 days at 10 s). Derived from on-chain data, not self-reported. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #45: Consensus timers are tied to a specific block and round. An old timer that fires late is simply ignored. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #45: Every timer in Pactus's v2 consensus is tagged with its height and round. A timer that fires after the node has moved on is simply dropped. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #46: Consensus follows the clock: a new block every 10 seconds. In the v2 code, a node whose clock runs a bit late catches up when it sees the others already voting. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #46: Consensus is paced on wall-clock time: the next height starts at last block time + the block interval (10 s by default). The v2 code skips the rest of the wait if it already sees 2f+1 precommit power for round 0, for nodes whose clock lags. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #47: One node can run several validators. They talk to each other inside the node instead of over the network. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #47: A Pactus node running several validator keys uses an in-process mediator: each proposal and vote is forwarded to its other local instances, and a block announcement moves them all to the next height. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #48: Pactus validators sign with BLS, a scheme where many signatures can be merged into one. That's why block proofs stay so small. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #48: Pactus validators sign with BLS12-381: 48-byte signatures (G1), 96-byte public keys (G2), hash-to-curve per the IRTF BLS draft with SHA-256. Signatures add up, which is what makes one-signature certificates possible. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #49: Pactus accounts support three signature types: BLS, Ed25519 and secp256k1 (Bitcoin's curve). The address tells which one is used. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #49: Pactus accounts can use three signature schemes: BLS12-381, Ed25519 and secp256k1. The signer's address type decides which one a transaction uses. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #50: Pactus addresses start with "pc1" on mainnet and "tpc1" on testnet, in bech32m, the same format Bitcoin uses for its newest addresses. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #50: Pactus addresses = RIPEMD-160(BLAKE2b-256(pubkey)) plus a 1-byte type, encoded as bech32m. HRP "pc" on mainnet, "tpc" on testnet. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #51: You can tell an address type at a glance: pc1p… is a validator, pc1z… a BLS account, pc1r… Ed25519, pc1y… secp256k1. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #51: The first character after "pc1" tells the account type in Pactus: pc1p… is a validator, pc1z… a BLS account, pc1r… Ed25519, pc1y… secp256k1. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #52: The treasury has a special address: all zeros. It can't sign transactions, so its funds only move through protocol rules, like block rewards. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #52: The Pactus treasury address isn't a bech32m string at all: it's the all-zero address, special-cased in encoding and decoding. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #53: Pactus wallets are HD wallets: one seed phrase recovers all your keys, organised by key type, with separate coin numbers for mainnet and testnet. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #53: Pactus HD paths: m/purpose'/coin'/type'/index. Purpose 12381 for BLS, 44 (BIP-44) for Ed25519 and secp256k1, 65535 for imported keys. Coin 21888 mainnet, 21777 testnet. Type = address type (1-4). Index is hardened except for BLS. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #54: A watch-only Pactus wallet, with no private keys at all, can still create new BLS addresses to receive funds. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #54: BLS HD keys (PIP-11): HMAC-SHA512 keyed with "BLS12381 seed"; the left half goes through BLS KeyGen, the right half is the chain code. Non-hardened children derive from the public key, so a watch-only wallet can create BLS addresses. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #55: Wallets are encrypted with Argon2id, a scheme built to resist password guessing. You can also make a watch-only copy that holds no private keys. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #55: Wallets encrypt with Argon2id (3 iterations, 64 MiB, 4 lanes), then AES-256-CTR with a 4-byte MAC. New wallets use SQLite (old JSON ones can be migrated), and `pactus-wallet neuter` makes a watch-only copy with no private keys. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #56: With PIP-50, an account can anchor data on chain: a fingerprint of the data plus a link to it, backed by a deposit of at least 1 PAC. Live once the network upgrades to protocol v5. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #56: With PIP-50 (protocol v5), a Pactus account can carry an anchor: a 32–64 byte root hash plus a URI of up to 128 bytes. Creating one locks a deposit of at least 1 PAC. Native on-chain state anchoring, live once >75% of committee power runs v5. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #57: Pactus has 7 built-in transaction types: transfer, stake, unstake, withdraw, committee claim, batch transfer and anchor. Each one is handled natively by the protocol. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #57: Pactus has 7 transaction types built into the protocol: transfer, bond, unbond, withdraw, sortition, batch transfer and anchor. Each has its own executor. Anchor only becomes valid once blocks reach protocol version 5 (PIP-50). #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #58: Fees are simple: a fixed 0.01 PAC by default, and unstaking is free. No bidding war to get your transaction in. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #58: Fees: the default minimum is a fixed 0.01 PAC for transfers, bonds, withdrawals, batch transfers and anchors; unbond and sortition are free. It's node mempool policy, not a consensus rule. Mempool is FIFO per type: no fee auction. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #59: An optional extra fee can kick in for accounts that send a lot of data in a day. It's off by default. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #59: Pactus has an optional consumption-based fee on top of the fixed one, driven by the bytes an account sent over the last 8,640 blocks. Past the 360-byte daily limit it grows faster than linearly. Unit price defaults to 0, so it's off. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #60: A transaction stays valid for about one day. Not included by then? It expires. Memos can be up to 64 bytes. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #60: In Pactus a transaction's lock time is also its expiry: it stays valid for 8,640 blocks (about 1 day at 10 s blocks; sortition txs get only 17). Memos are capped at 64 bytes. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #61: A batch transfer pays 2 to 8 people in one transaction, for a single fee. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #61: A Pactus batch transfer pays 2 to 8 distinct recipients in one signed transaction. The sender pays the total plus a single fee. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #62: The waiting room for transactions (the mempool) has a separate lane per type, so a flood of transfers can't crowd out staking or other transactions. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #62: Pactus's mempool has one bounded sub-pool per transaction type. With the default max_size of 1,000, transfers get 500 slots and each of the other six types 100, so the pool holds up to 1,100 txs. A full sub-pool drops its oldest entry. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #63: Block proposers pick waiting transactions in a fixed order by type, then first come, first served. No fee auction. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #63: Pactus's proposer takes mempool txs in a fixed type order: sortition, bond, unbond, withdraw, transfer, batch, anchor; first in, first out within a type. It re-checks them, caps the block at 1,000 txs and puts the subsidy tx first. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #64: The whole chain state, all accounts and validators, is summed up in one fingerprint stored in every block. Updating it only reworks the parts that changed. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #64: Pactus's state root combines two incremental Merkle trees, one for accounts and one for validators, hashed with BLAKE2b-256. A block only rehashes the paths of the leaves it changed. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #65: Every account and validator gets a sequential number when it's created, which is also its place in that state fingerprint. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #65: Every Pactus account and validator gets a sequential number at creation. That number is also its leaf position in the Merkle state tree. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #66: Each block is saved in one atomic write: if a node crashes mid-save, it never ends up half-updated. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #66: Pactus commits each block in a single LevelDB batch: block bytes, tx index, account and validator updates, public keys, last certificate. A crash can't leave them out of sync. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #67: Looking up a transaction is quick: the node knows exactly where it sits inside its block. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #67: Pactus's tx index stores (height, offset, length) per transaction ID. Reading a transaction slices the stored block bytes directly, without decoding the whole block. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #68: Public keys are stored once per account instead of in every transaction, which saves disk space. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #68: Each signer's public key lives in a separate index. After a signer's first appearance, its txs are stored without the public key in the block bytes, and the key is restored from the index when you read the block or tx. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #69: Short on disk space? A node can be pruned to keep only the last 30 days of blocks (10 days minimum). Nodes keep full history unless you choose to prune. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #69: Prune mode: default retention is 30 days of blocks (259,200 at 10 s), minimum 10 days. `pactus-daemon prune` converts an existing full node to prune mode. A node syncing from genesis keeps full history unless you prune it. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #70: Catching up is pull-based: a node that falls behind asks peers for the blocks it misses. Gossip is only for fresh news: new blocks, transactions and votes. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #70: Pactus sync is pull-based by design: a node that falls behind asks peers for blocks over direct streams instead of being sent them. Gossip is for fresh data only: new-block announcements, transactions and consensus messages. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #71: Pactus nodes gossip on three channels: blocks, transactions and consensus. Each network has its own channel names, so mainnet and testnet never mix. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #71: Pactus gossip runs on three libp2p gossipsub topics: block, transaction, consensus. Topic names carry the network name, so networks stay separated at the libp2p level. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #72: All Pactus network messages share one envelope format, and each message type knows whether it's broadcast or sent to a single peer. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #72: Every Pactus P2P message travels in the same CBOR envelope: flags, message type, payload, consensus height. Each message type declares whether it's gossiped or sent point to point. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #73: A node catching up downloads from several peers at once: up to 8 parallel batches of 720 blocks. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #73: A Pactus node catching up opens up to 8 parallel download sessions of 720 blocks each; the serving peer answers in 60-block messages. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #74: Blocks may arrive out of order, but they are always added to the chain in order, each with its proof. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #74: Pactus syncs in parallel but commits in strict order: downloaded blocks wait in an LRU cache keyed by height, and are committed only when the next height and its certificate are present. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #75: For downloads, nodes favour peers that delivered reliably, while still giving the others a chance. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #75: Block-download peers are picked at random, weighted by track record: score = (completed+1)/(total+1) sessions, never below 1%. New peers start at the top; failing peers rarely get picked but stay selectable. Only handshaken peers qualify. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #76: Very far behind, about 10 days or more? A node then downloads only from peers that keep the full history. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #76: Pactus nodes advertise a FULL flag if they keep the whole chain history. A node more than 86,400 blocks (about 10 days) behind downloads only from FULL peers; within that window any handshaken peer, pruned or full, can serve it. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #77: Before exchanging blocks, two nodes say hello and acknowledge each other. Only peers that complete this handshake are used for syncing. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #77: Handshake: the outbound peer sends Hello; the inbound peer replies with a HelloAck and its own Hello; the outbound peer acks it. A peer is "known" only after both Hellos are accepted, and only known peers request or serve blocks. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #78: Behind a home router? Pactus nodes detect it and use relays and hole punching to stay reachable. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #78: Pactus nodes behind NAT use libp2p AutoNAT v2 to detect reachability, then fall back to relays with hole punching. UPnP is opt-in. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #79: Nodes cap their connections (64 by default, fewer outgoing) and reconnect automatically if they drop below a minimum. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #79: Pactus caps connections by direction: inbound up to 64 by default (max_connections), outbound a quarter of that (16). Every 60s, if fewer than 14 peers (64/4 - 2) are connected, it redials its saved and bootstrap peers in the background. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #80: A node remembers its peers when it shuts down cleanly and reconnects to them at the next start. The mainnet bootstrap list is built in. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #80: A Pactus node saves the peers it has connected to, plus bootstrap entries, to peers.json on clean shutdown and reloads them next to the bootstrap list at startup. Mainnet's bootstrap list is embedded in the binary. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #81: The node's API is defined once, and gRPC, REST, JSON-RPC and the docs are all generated from that single definition. One source, always in sync. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #81: The Pactus node API is defined once in `.proto` files. One `buf generate` emits gRPC stubs, a REST gateway, JSON-RPC bindings, OpenAPI, OpenRPC and docs. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #82: Out of the box, a mainnet node only opens its main API to the local machine. Everything else is opt-in. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #82: Pactus's node gRPC API: 5 services, 54 RPCs. The wallet service is opt-in (enable_wallet=false). With mainnet defaults only gRPC is on, bound to 127.0.0.1:50051; REST, JSON-RPC and ZeroMQ are off. (Testnet defaults differ.) #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #83: Developers also get JSON-RPC and REST, with an interactive Swagger page built into the node. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #83: Pactus's JSON-RPC server is a thin layer over the node's own gRPC server, and the REST gateway ships with a Swagger UI embedded in the binary via `go:embed`. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #84: Apps can subscribe to a live feed of new blocks and transactions over ZeroMQ. Off by default. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #84: Nodes can publish committed blocks and their txs on ZeroMQ: 5 feeds (block info, tx info, raw block, raw tx, anchor info), each tagged with a 2-byte topic ID. Off by default. Pure-Go zmq4, no libzmq. Raw block = header only. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #85: pactus-shell lets you query a node from the command line, with an interactive mode. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #85: `pactus-shell` is a gRPC CLI with an interactive prompt mode. Its commands are generated from the same `.proto` services as the gRPC API, so it follows the API once the code is regenerated and rebuilt. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #86: The wallet can talk to your own node, to public servers, or work fully offline. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #86: The Pactus wallet talks to the chain through a provider: a local node, a remote gRPC server list, or offline mode with no network calls at all. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #87: Two nodes can't accidentally run on the same data folder: the second one refuses to start. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #87: `pactus-daemon` takes an exclusive file lock on its working directory before starting or pruning. A second instance on the same data prints a warning and exits. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #88: The official Docker image is small: static binaries on plain Alpine Linux. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #88: The Pactus Docker image is a two-stage build: static binaries (CGO off, `-trimpath`, stripped) copied into plain Alpine. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #89: Pactus tests are reproducible: random test data comes from a logged seed, and integration tests spin up a small 4-node network. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #89: Test helpers draw random values (keys, heights, amounts, blocks) from a seed each test logs. To reproduce a failure, build the suite with NewTestSuiteFromSeed and that seed. Integration tests boot four in-process nodes with fixed keys. #PAC @PactusChain

simple: Inside #Pactus #90: Version checks ignore tags like "beta": 1.18.0-beta counts as 1.18.0. #PAC @PactusChain
tech: Inside #Pactus #90: Pactus compares versions by major.minor.patch only: "1.18.0-beta" ranks the same as 1.18.0. A deliberate departure from SemVer, with the version baked in at build time. #PAC @PactusChain
